title: open-top cylinder minimum area
stem: An open-top cylindrical tank must contain 8π cubic meters. Its circular base and curved side use the same material. What radius and height minimize the material area, and what does that result mean for the tank?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Radius 1 m and height 8 m; this is the least material area.
choices.rationale: These dimensions meet the volume requirement, but the area derivative is negative at radius 1, so a larger radius uses less material.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Radius 2 m and height 2 m; this is the least material area among positive dimensions holding 8π m³.
choices.rationale: Correct: From πr²h=8π, h=8/r² and S(r)=πr²+16π/r. S'(r)=2πr−16π/r² vanishes only at r³=8, so r=2 and h=2. The area tends to infinity at both positive-domain ends, so this is the global minimum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radius 4 m and height 0.5 m; this is the least material area.
choices.rationale: Doubling the optimal radius keeps the volume but increases area; the area derivative is positive there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radius 6 m and height 2/9 m; this is the least material area.
choices.rationale: Tripling the optimal radius makes a much wider, shallower tank and increases material area.

title: two-pen fence maximum area
stem: A farmer has 120 meters of fencing for a rectangular field and one interior fence parallel to the two shorter sides, making two pens. The interior fence spans the field's width. What field dimensions give the greatest total enclosed area, and what is that area?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Width 30 m, length 15 m; total area 450 m².
choices.rationale: This feasible width lies past the vertex of the concave area function, so its area is smaller.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Width 20 m, length 30 m; maximum total area 600 m².
choices.rationale: Correct: With width w and length l, 3w+2l=120. Thus A(w)=w(120−3w)/2, 0<w<40. The quadratic is concave and A'=(120−6w)/2=0 at w=20; l=30, giving 600 m².

choices.label: C
choices.text: Width 10 m, length 45 m; total area 450 m².
choices.rationale: This feasible width lies before the vertex, so its area is smaller.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Width 30 m, length 30 m; total area 900 m².
choices.rationale: A square of those dimensions requires more fencing once the interior divider is included.

title: linear-demand maximum profit
stem: A shop can sell q=100−2p items per week when each sells for p dollars, where demand is positive. The variable cost is $10 per item and there is no fixed cost. Which price maximizes weekly profit, and what maximum profit does the model predict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Price $25; maximum profit equals revenue, so $1250 per week.
choices.rationale: This maximizes revenue p·q but ignores the per-item cost, so it does not maximize profit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Price $10; maximum profit $0 per week.
choices.rationale: Pricing at marginal cost gives zero profit, while the interior critical price gives positive profit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Price $30; maximum profit $800 per week.
choices.rationale: Correct: Profit is P(p)=(p−10)(100−2p). Its derivative is 120−4p, which is zero at p=30; the second derivative is −4<0. Then q=40 and P=800. This price lies in the feasible positive-demand interval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Price $50; maximum profit $0 per week.
choices.rationale: At this price demand is zero, so profit is zero rather than maximal.
